Case report

AL amyloidosis manifesting as a vertebral amyloidoma secondary to an unrecognized plasmacytoma expressing cyclin D1 case report

Jeremy B. Jones a, Nicolas Lopez-Hisijos a, Richard A. Berkman b, Justin T. Kelley a,*

a Department of Pathology, Microbiology and Immunology, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, United States of America b Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, United States of America

A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: AL amyloidosis Amyloidoma Spine Cyclin D1 Case report

A B S T R A C T

Introduction: Immunoglobin-related (AL) amyloidosis is the production of amyloidogenic immunoglobulin light chains from clonal plasma cells or, rarely, B-cell lymphomas with plasmacytic differentiation. Amyloid deposition causes progressive end organ destruction with profound morbidity. Presentation of case: We present a rare case of a lambda light chain AL amyloidoma localized to a thoracic vertebra of an 87-year-old woman who had a remote history of an unspecified non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma (NHL). Our patient presented with upper extremity neuropathy and was found by MRI to have a malignant-appearing lesion throughout the T1 vertebra. Initial biopsy showed amyloid deposition and staging evaluation found localized disease. Prior to planned surgery and radiation the following year, she had worsening neuropathy including multiple falls. Repeat MRI confirmed lesion progression with concern for cord compression. Urgent surgical resection was performed. Histology showed numerous plasma cells with abundant amyloid deposition that was found by amyloid typing to be lambda light chain. An incidental B-cell rich lymphoid aggregate was also seen in a bone marrow fragment that required additional immunohistochemical evaluation, showing the aggregate to be benign while revealing the plasma cells to be positive for cyclin D1. She received localized radiation and has been asymptomatic. Discussion: Amyloidosis and plasma cell neoplasms require appropriate staging evaluation. The cyclin D1-positive plasma cells raises the possibility of the t(11;14)/IGH::CCND1 translocation that portends better prognosis and therapeutic response with venetoclax. Conclusion: Amyloidomas are uncommon and may present in nearly any site, requiring a high index of clinical suspicion for proper diagnosis.

1. Introduction

Amyloidosis is the deposition of misfolded proteins that form insoluble aggregates in extracellular tissue, resulting in organ damage. Amyloid consists of continuous, nonbranching fibrils with a diameter of approximately 7.5–10 nm that are composed of stacked beta-sheet motifs arranged perpendicular to the axis of the fibril. Histologically, amyloid appears as amorphous eosinophilic extracellular deposits that stains with Congo red and shows a characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light. The uniform physical properties of amyloid produce a number of similar, although unique, diseases [1,2]. Amyloid is associated with a variety of inflammatory, inherited and neoplastic conditions [3]. At least 42 amyloidogenic proteins have been

described in humans, and are broadly classified as localized, systemic and hereditary. Systemic amyloidosis may also be classified as primary if due to immunoglobulin light chain deposition from an underlying neoplastic process (AL amyloidosis), or secondary if due to serum amyloid-associated (SAA) protein deposition from underlying chronic inflammation (AA amyloidosis). The common sites and distribution of disease vary by the amyloid subtype, but are all typically found in thickened blood vessel walls, basement membranes, periosteal tissue and soft tissue interstitium [1,4,5]. Laser microdissection and mass spectrometry (LDMS) is the most effective method of typing the amyloid protein, with nearly 100 % sensitivity and specificity [6]. Amyloidoma, a localized mass of amyloid deposition, is a rare manifestation of amyloidosis, especially in an isolated vertebra. Here,

units.text:
J.B. Jones et al.

International Journal of Surgery Case Reports 121 (2024) 110000

we present a unique case of a vertebral AL amyloidoma in an 87-year-old woman due to a previously undiagnosed plasmacytoma with cyclin D1 expression by immunohistochemistry. We aim to emphasize the appropriate staging evaluation of amyloidosis and plasma cell neoplasms, including amyloid typing and plasma cell neoplasm genetic evaluation. We will also briefly overview the evaluation of incidental lymphoid aggregates in the bone marrow.

2. Presentation of case

2.2. Disease progression and surgical resection

Over the next year prior to surgery, she had worsening fatigue, atrial fibrillation and neuropathy with multiple falls, prompting repeat imaging. MRI then showed progression of her T1 spinal lesion with concern for cord compression. She was urgently seen by neurosurgery and underwent a decompressive thoracic laminectomy at T1 and C7 with partial removal of T1, resection of C7-T1, decompression of the left C8 nerve root and cervical thoracic fixation and fusion from C5-T3.

2.1. Initial presentation and evaluation

The patient is an 87-year-old woman with a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, chronic atrial fibrillation and an unspecified non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) of the right tonsil status post tonsillectomy and radiation treatment 15 years prior. She initially presented with complaints of worsening left upper extremity pain and paresthesia, and was found by MRI (Fig. 1A) to have an expansile malignant-appearing lesion throughout the T1 vertebral body and posterior elements with severe spinal stenosis. A CT-guided core biopsy (Fig. 1C-D) was composed entirely of amyloid with a foreign-body giant cell reaction. Staging evaluation was subsequently performed. Laboratory findings were remarkable for an elevated kappa/lambda ratio of 2.3 with increased free kappa (6.7 mg/dL) and free lambda (3.1 mg/dL) light chains. No monoclonal protein was identified by serum or urine protein electrophoresis (SPEP and UPEP, respectively) and immunofixation (IFIX), and a bone marrow biopsy was negative for a plasma cell neoplasm. PET imaging (Fig. 1B) confirmed localized uptake in the T1 vertebra. She was diagnosed with a localized amyloidoma, presumed AL amyloidosis, with plan for resection and post-operative radiation therapy the following year.

2.3. Pathologic evaluation

Histology was remarkable for abundant amorphous eosinophilic material infiltrating bone, skeletal muscle and ligaments (Fig. 2A-D). The eosinophilic deposits were positive with Congo red and showed apple-green birefringence with polarization (Fig. 2E-F). CD138 highlighted numerous plasma cells around the amyloid deposits (Fig. 3A-B). Kappa and lambda immunohistochemistry (IHC) and in-situ hybridization (ISH) were unsuccessful due to extensive decalcification. The bone marrow fragments did not show increased plasma cells by morphology or IHC, and the blood vessels were unremarkable (Fig. 3C-D). One bone marrow fragment, however, showed a single small lymphoid aggregate. The lymphoid aggregate was B-cell rich with CD3 and CD20 (Fig. 3E-F), and was negative for CD5, CD10 and cyclin D1. Cyclin D1, however, was incidentally positive in the plasma cells (Fig. 3B inset). No ancillary studies, including flow cytometry, were performed. Amyloid typing by LDMS confirmed immunoglobulin lambda light chain.

2.4. Staging and treatment

Follow-up staging evaluation with establishment of AL amyloidosis was remarkable for a transient tiny monoclonal free kappa light chain by UPEP with IFIX. An endomyocardial biopsy was negative for amyloid deposition. She then received localized radiation to the involved site and

3. Discussion

We present a rare case of AL amyloidosis manifesting as an isolated vertebral amyloidoma due to an unrecognized plasmacytoma with incidental cyclin D1 expression by immunohistochemistry. The patient is an 87-year-old woman with RA, chronic atrial fibrillation and a remote NHL, who suffered progressive morbidity due to amyloid accumulation. Biopsy and subsequent resection revealed abundant amyloid deposition, which was surrounded by numerous cyclin D1-positive plasma cells. LDMS confirmed lambda light chain amyloid, and staging evaluation, including PET imaging, bone marrow biopsy, endomyocardial biopsy and protein electrophoresis, confirmed localized disease. She received localized radiation with improvement and remains asymptomatic. Amyloid deposition leads to a “waxy” gross appearance of affected tissue, and causes symptoms related to tissue infiltration and damage. Examples include arrythmias and heart failure with preserved ejection

fraction in the heart, renal dysfunction and proteinuria in the kidney, macroglossia in the tongue, periorbital purpura in the eye, malabsorption and hepatosplenomaly in the gut, neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome in peripheral and autonomic nerves and spinal cord compression in the spine. These findings are characteristic but nonspecific of amyloid, requiring a high index of clinical suspicion [7]. However, patients may be asymptomatic with incidental discovery by routine or other imaging [8,9]. Amyloidomas are uncommon in amyloidosis. They are a solitary mass of amyloid, similar to solitary plasmacytomas in plasma cell neoplasms, and can occur anywhere in the body [7,8,10–12]. Isolated spinal amyloidomas are remarkably rare with only few reported cases [13–19], with a mean age at presentation of 62 years and a 2:1 male-to-female ratio [19]. Like our case, approximately 95 % of spinal amyloidomas are composed of AL amyloid [19], with rare cases composed of beta 2- microglobulin amyloid [14,19] and a single case of transthyretin amyloid [20]. While IHC and/or ISH are reliable surrogates, LDMS remains the most effective amyloid typing method for proper classification, treatment, prognosis and possible genetic counseling. In a comparison study of IHC and LDMS [21], there was 100 % concordance between the methods. However, IHC and ISH may be unsuccessful in approximately

25 % of cases [21], such as in our case, necessitating LDMS. AL amyloidosis is uncommon with an annual incidence of 1/100,000 per year. It is caused by immunoglobulin light chain deposition by clonal plasma cells or, less frequently, B-cell lymphomas with plasmacytic differentiation. The majority (>80 %) show free lambda light chain, with the remaining showing free kappa light chain [7]. Clonal plasma cells show similar immunophenotypic aberrancies as plasma cell neoplasms, such as aberrant expression of CD56 or cyclin D1, which is present in about 50 % of cases each [7,22]. Progression from localized to systemic AL amyloidosis occurs in 1 % or fewer of cases, while 17–44 % of cases demonstrate recurrence or local progression [8,9]. Translocations involving IGH and one of the cyclin genes (CCND1, CCND2 or CCND3) are recurring genetic abnormalities in plasma cell neoplasms, and are considered primary genetic events in disease pathogenesis [23]. The t(11;14)/IGH::CCND1 translocation constitutively activates the CCND1 locus with the IGH promoter, resulting in overexpression of cyclin D1. Cyclin D1 overexpression offers a proliferative advantage by inactivating the tumor suppressor protein Rb, allowing cell cycle progression from G1 to S in the cell cycle [24]. Cyclin D1 can be detected by IHC and used as a marker for the translocation. However,

cyclin D1 expression is not specific for t(11;14), which can be upregulated via multiple mechanisms, such as increased copy number of the locus or chromosome [25–28]. General standard of care therapy targets the neoplastic plasma cell clone. For localized disease, targeted radiation is standard management [29]. For systemic disease, daratumumab, an anti-CD38 monoclonal therapeutic antibody, and autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation, if eligible, become standard care [30]. In multiple myeloma, t(11;14)/IGH::CCND1 is associated with better prognosis [31] and good response to venetoclax [32], a BCL2 inhibitor, which is upregulated by an unknown mechanism in the translocation [33]. Bortezomib, a proteosome inhibitor, is standard therapy for high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities, producing similar outcomes as standard risk patients. In AL amyloidosis, bortezomib-based regimens are typically offered to patients with high-risk clinical status. However, bortezomib demonstrates poor response in t(11;14)-positive patients [34]. This impact of cytogenetic findings on therapy and prognosis emphasizes the importance of evaluating genetic aberrations in plasma cell neoplasms, including AL amyloidosis, particularly if chemotherapy is indicated. targeted removal of the amyloid fibril deposits. Multiple clinical trials have been attempted, and current phase III studies for cardiac AL amyloid are actively recruiting for both CAEL101 and birtamimab, both anti-IgG1 monoclonal antibodies, in combination with standard of care versus standard of care alone. Additional approaches are also being attempted, including early attempts at light chain stabilizers to suppress formation of toxic deposits [35]. Further remarkable about this case is that the patient had a remote history of an unspecified NHL, and was found to have an incidental B-cell rich lymphoid aggregate in one of the resection bone marrow fragments. Small T-cell rich lymphoid aggregates are common in the bone marrow of older individuals, but B-cell rich lymphoid aggregates are unusual and require exclusion of a B-cell lymphoma. Other concerning features of lymphoid aggregates in the bone marrow include large size (>600 μm), infiltrative borders, cellular atypia and paratrabecular location. As the number of concerning features increases, the odds of malignancy increases [36,37]. Aside from the B-cell rich pattern, the lymphoid aggregate in our case was otherwise unremarkable with small size, smooth border, no cellular atypia and interstitial location. Additionally, staging evaluation for the AL amyloidoma revealed no other sites of disease, supporting a benign lymphoid aggregate.

4. Conclusion

A high index of suspicion and appropriate workup, including staging with cytogenetic studies and amyloid typing, are crucial to guide correct diagnosis, therapy and prognosis in AL amyloidosis.

Ethical approval

This work has been reported in line with the SCARE criteria [38]. All patient information and material are deidentified. The patient expressly consents to publication, and written consent can be provided upon request. Ethics approval is not required for case reports at our institution.
